items.title: py-buzz
items.text:
That's not flying, it's falling with style: Exceptions with extras

Long ago, I found myself writing the same boilerplate for condition checks and exception wrappers over and over. So I gathered some helpers together to cut down on repetitive error-handling code. When I switched projects later, I wanted those helpers there, too! That's how py-buzz came to be.

Now, I have a collection of really useful exception helpers that I can use in all my projects, and I'm sharing them with you!

items.title: Getting started
items.text:
Python 3.11 or newer is required, and installation takes one line:

uv add py-buzz

Here's a small example with a project-specific exception:

from buzz import Buzz


class ConfigError(Buzz):
    pass


def read_port(value: object) -> int:
    port = ConfigError.ensure_type(value, int, "Port must be an integer")
    ConfigError.require_condition(1 <= port <= 65535, "Port must be between 1 and 65535")
    return port


def parse_port(value: str) -> int:
    with ConfigError.handle_errors("Couldn't parse the configured port"):
        port = int(value)
    return read_port(port)

Here, ensure_type() checks the value at runtime and returns it with a narrowed type, while require_condition() raises ConfigError if the port is out of range. handle_errors() gives parsing failures a bit more context by wrapping the original ValueError in a ConfigError.

items.title: What's in the box
items.text:
Most helpers come in two flavors: standalone functions that work with regular exception types and methods on a Buzz subclass that raise that class. reformat_exception() is a standalone helper for formatting exception messages.

  • require_condition() checks a condition.
  • enforce_defined() rejects None and narrows the value's type.
  • ensure_type() checks a runtime type and narrows the result.
  • verify_literal() checks a Literal value.
  • handle_errors() and handle_errors_async() add context to exceptions from a block.
  • Buzz.retry() and Buzz.retry_async() retry synchronous and asynchronous operations.
  • check_expressions() reports multiple failed checks together.
  • raise_from() adds context while preserving the original exception as the cause.
  • reformat_exception() formats an exception message with more context.
  • get_traceback() fetches the current traceback.

The standalone retry() and retry_async() decorators live in buzz.tools; the retry guide shows both styles.

items.title: The demos
items.text:
The optional demo extra bundles executable examples of the features. With uv, the demos can run in an isolated environment:

uvx --from='py-buzz[demo]' py-buzz-demo

The demo guide has a few more ways to run individual examples.

items.title: Demo
items.text: The optional demo extra comes with executable examples of the py-buzz helpers. Each one shows how a helper shapes exception handling and program flow.

items.title: Installation
items.text:
The demo is an optional extra, so it joins py-buzz when the package is installed with:

uv pip install 'py-buzz[demo]'

items.title: Running the demo
items.text:
Installing the extra also adds a demo entrypoint:

py-buzz-demo

With no arguments, the entrypoint runs all available demos. To focus on one feature, the --feature=<feature> option selects its demos.

The full list of options is available with:

py-buzz-demo --help

items.title: Running the demo in an isolated environment with uv
items.text:
The demo can run through uv without adding its dependencies to your system Python or an activated virtual environment:

uvx --from='py-buzz[demo]' py-buzz-demo

items.text:

items.title: check_expressions
items.text:
check_expressions(base_message: str, raise_exc_class: type[Exception] = Exception, raise_args: Iterable[Any] | None = None, raise_kwargs: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None, exc_builder: Callable[[ExcBuilderParams], Exception] = default_exc_builder, do_except: ExceptionCallback | None = None, do_else: NoArgCallback | None = None)

Check a series of expressions inside of a context manager. If any fail an exception is raised that contains a main message and a description of each failing expression.

Parameters:

  • base_message (str) –

    The base failure message to include in the constructed message that is passed to the raised Exception. Will be included in ExcBuilderParams passed to exc_builder.

  • raise_exc_class (type[Exception], default: Exception ) –

    The exception type to raise with the assembled message if any of the expressions are falsey.

               Defaults to Exception.

           May not be None.
  • raise_args (Iterable[Any] | None, default: None ) –

    Additional positional args (after the assembled message) that will passed when raising an instance of the raise_exc_class.

  • raise_kwargs (Mapping[str, Any] | None, default: None ) –

    Keyword args that will be passed when raising an instance of the raise_exc_class.

  • exc_builder (Callable[[ExcBuilderParams], Exception], default: default_exc_builder ) –

    A function that should be called to construct the raised raise_exc_class. Useful for exception classes that do not take a message as the first positional argument.

  • do_except (ExceptionCallback | None, default: None ) –

    A function that should be called only if the any of the expressions are falsey. Must accept one parameter that is the exception that will be raised. If not provided, nothing will be done.

  • do_else (NoArgCallback | None, default: None ) –

    A function that should be called if none of the the expressions are falsey. If not provided, nothing will be done.

Example:

The following is an example usage::

    with check_expressions("Something wasn't right") as check:
        check(a is not None)
        check(a > b, "a must be greater than b")
        check(a != 1, "a must not equal 1")
        check(b >= 0, "b must not be negative")

This would render output like::

    Checked expressions failed: Something wasn't right:
      1: first expressoin failed
      3: a must not equal 1

items.title: handle_errors
items.text:
handle_errors(base_message: str, raise_exc_class: type[Exception] | None = Exception, raise_args: Iterable[Any] | None = None, raise_kwargs: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None, handle_exc_class: type[BaseException] | tuple[type[BaseException], ...] = Exception, ignore_exc_class: type[BaseException] | tuple[type[BaseException], ...] | None = None, do_finally: NoArgCallback | None = None, do_except: DoExceptParamsCallback | None = None, do_else: NoArgCallback | None = None, exc_builder: Callable[[ExcBuilderParams], Exception] = default_exc_builder) -> Iterator[None]

Provide a context manager that will intercept exceptions and repackage them in a new exception with a message attached that combines the base message along with the message from the handled exception:

Parameters:

  • base_message (str) –

    The base message to attach to the raised exception. Will be included in ExcBuilderParams passed to exc_builder.

  • raise_exc_class (type[Exception] | None, default: Exception ) –

    The exception type to raise with the constructed message if an exception is caught in the managed context. If None is passed, no new exception will be raised and only the do_except, do_else, and do_finally functions will be called.

  • raise_args (Iterable[Any] | None, default: None ) –

    Additional positional args (after the constructed message) that will passed when raising an instance of the raise_exc_class.

  • raise_kwargs (Mapping[str, Any] | None, default: None ) –

    Keyword args that will be passed when raising an instance of the raise_exc_class.

  • handle_exc_class (type[BaseException] | tuple[type[BaseException], ...], default: Exception ) –

    Limits the class of exceptions that will be intercepted Any other exception types will not be caught and re-packaged. Defaults to Exception (will handle all exceptions). May also be provided as a tuple of multiple exception types to handle.

  • ignore_exc_class (type[BaseException] | tuple[type[BaseException], ...] | None, default: None ) –

    Defines an exception or set of exception types that should not be handled at all. Any matching exception types will be immediately re-raised. They will not be handled by the handle_errors context manager at all. This is useful if you want a specific variant of your handle_exc_class to not be handled by handle_errors. For example, if you want to use handle_exc_class=Exception but you do not want handle_errors to handle RuntimeError. Then, you would set ignore_exc_class=RuntimeError.

  • do_finally (NoArgCallback | None, default: None ) –

    A function that should always be called at the end of the block. Should take no parameters. If not provided, nothing will be done.

  • do_except (DoExceptParamsCallback | None, default: None ) –

    A function that should be called only if there was an exception. Must accept one parameter that is an instance of the DoExceptParams dataclass. Note that the do_except method is passed the original exception. If not provided, nothing will be done.

  • do_else (NoArgCallback | None, default: None ) –

    A function that should be called only if there were no exceptions encountered. If not provided, nothing will be done.

  • exc_builder (Callable[[ExcBuilderParams], Exception], default: default_exc_builder ) –

    A function that should be called to construct the raised raise_exc_class. Useful for exception classes that do not take a message as the first positional argument.

Example:

The following is an example usage:

    with handle_errors("It didn't work"):
        some_code_that_might_raise_an_exception()

items.title: Check multiple expressions
items.text: The check_expressions() context manager gathers the results of multiple checks in a block. Any failures appear together in one exception at the end; when every check passes, no exception is raised.

items.title: Basic use
items.text:
from buzz import check_expressions

with check_expressions("there will be errors") as check:
    check(True)
    check(False)
    check(1 == 2, "one is not two")
    check('cooooooool', 'not a problem')
    check(0, "zero is still zero")

The example raises an exception like this:

Exception: Checked expressions failed: there will be errors
   2: 2nd expression failed
   3: one is not two
   5: zero is still zero

A Buzz subclass method uses the same checks and raises that subclass:

from buzz import Buzz

class ConfigError(Buzz):
    pass

with ConfigError.check_expressions("there will be errors") as check:
    check(False, "configuration is invalid")

items.title: Advanced use
items.text:
The standalone check_expressions() function lets you customize how the combined failure is constructed. The builder receives base_message as well as the assembled message and constructor arguments, and must forward those fields to the exception constructor:

from buzz import Buzz, check_expressions
from buzz.tools import ExcBuilderParams


class ValidationError(Exception):
    def __init__(self, message: str, phase: str, *, source: str, base_message: str):
        self.phase = phase
        self.source = source
        self.base_message = base_message
        super().__init__(message)


def build_validation_error(params: ExcBuilderParams) -> Exception:
    return params.raise_exc_class(
        params.message,
        *params.raise_args,
        base_message=params.base_message,
        **params.raise_kwargs,
    )


def report_failure(exc: Exception) -> None:
    print(f"Validation failed: {exc}")


def report_success() -> None:
    print("Configuration passed validation")


def validate_config(config: object) -> None:
    with check_expressions(
        "Invalid configuration",
        raise_exc_class=ValidationError,
        raise_args=["startup"],
        raise_kwargs={"source": "environment"},
        exc_builder=build_validation_error,
        do_except=report_failure,
        do_else=report_success,
    ) as check:
        check(hasattr(config, "host"), "host is required")
        check(getattr(config, "port", 0) > 0, "port must be positive")

Here do_except receives the constructed exception itself, not a DoExceptParams object. The first failed expression or both checks failing produces one ValidationError, with phase="startup", source="environment", and the "Invalid configuration" base message. If every check passes, do_else runs instead.

A Buzz subclass method binds its own exception class and builder, so it does not accept raise_exc_class or exc_builder:

class ValidationBuzzError(Buzz):
    def __init__(self, message: str, phase: str, *, source: str, base_message: str | None = None):
        self.phase = phase
        self.source = source
        super().__init__(message, base_message=base_message)


with ValidationBuzzError.check_expressions(
    "Invalid configuration",
    raise_args=["startup"],
    raise_kwargs={"source": "environment"},
    do_except=report_failure,
    do_else=report_success,
) as check:
    check(hasattr(config, "host"), "host is required")
    check(getattr(config, "port", 0) > 0, "port must be positive")

The context manager evaluates checks synchronously as they are called.

items.title: Enforce a defined value
items.text: enforce_defined() checks that a value is not None, raising an exception otherwise. It also narrows the value's type, which keeps static type checkers happy when you call a method on it.

items.title: Basic use
items.text:
from buzz import enforce_defined

# Vanilla Python
def vanilla(val: str | None) -> str:
    if val is None:
        raise ValueError("Received an undefined value!")
    return val.upper()

# With py-buzz
def buzzy(val: str | None) -> str:
    return enforce_defined(val).upper()

When the value is None, enforce_defined() raises an exception with a simple default message. A custom message is available through the message keyword argument.

A Buzz subclass method binds the exception type:

from buzz import Buzz, enforce_defined

class ConfigError(Buzz):
    pass

value = enforce_defined(config_value, "Missing config value", raise_exc_class=ConfigError)
value = ConfigError.enforce_defined(config_value, "Missing config value")

items.title: Advanced use
items.text:
A custom exception can carry the identity and source of a missing value. The standalone function takes an explicit non-Buzz exception class; the Buzz method binds its own class and exception builder while still accepting constructor arguments and callbacks:

from buzz import Buzz, enforce_defined


class MissingValueError(Exception):
    def __init__(self, message: str, field: str, *, source: str):
        self.field = field
        self.source = source
        super().__init__(message)


def report_missing(exc: Exception) -> None:
    print(f"Missing configuration: {exc}")


def report_present() -> None:
    print("Configuration value is present")


def read_database_url(value: str | None) -> str:
    return enforce_defined(
        value,
        "A database URL is required",
        raise_exc_class=MissingValueError,
        raise_args=["database_url"],
        raise_kwargs={"source": "environment"},
        do_except=report_missing,
        do_else=report_present,
    )


class MissingValueBuzzError(Buzz):
    def __init__(self, message: str, field: str, *, source: str, base_message: str | None = None):
        self.field = field
        self.source = source
        super().__init__(message, base_message=base_message)


def read_database_url_with_buzz(value: str | None) -> str:
    return MissingValueBuzzError.enforce_defined(
        value,
        "A database URL is required",
        raise_args=["database_url"],
        raise_kwargs={"source": "environment"},
        do_except=report_missing,
        do_else=report_present,
    )

For None, each function calls report_missing with the constructed exception, then raises it with field="database_url" and source="environment". For a defined value, report_present runs and the value is returned with its narrowed type. The standalone function also accepts exc_builder for constructors that need a different argument mapping; the Buzz method uses the class's builder automatically.

items.title: Ensure a value has the right type
items.text: ensure_type() checks that a value has the expected runtime type and raises an exception if it does not. On success, it returns the value with a narrowed type, which helps static type checkers follow along.
path: Ensure a value has the right type

items.title: Basic use
items.text:
from buzz import ensure_type

# Vanilla python
def vanilla(val: str | int) -> str:
    if not isinstance(val, str):
        raise Exception("Received a non-string value!")
    return val.upper()

# With py-buzz
def buzzy(val: str | int) -> str:
    return ensure_type(val, str).upper()

ensure_type() checks the runtime type; it does not cast the value. A basic message explains when the value has the wrong type, and the message keyword argument lets you provide a custom one.

A Buzz subclass method binds the exception type, so its call is shorter:

from buzz import Buzz, ensure_type

class ConfigError(Buzz):
    pass

name = ensure_type(config_value, str, "Expected a string", raise_exc_class=ConfigError)
name = ConfigError.ensure_type(config_value, str, "Expected a string")
path: Ensure a value has the right type

items.title: Advanced use
items.text:
Use a custom non-Buzz exception to record which field failed validation, and callbacks to distinguish rejection from success. Both forms below pass an explicit message; the Buzz.ensure_type() default currently contains the literal {type_} rather than formatting the expected type into it.

from buzz import Buzz, ensure_type


class TypeValidationError(Exception):
    def __init__(self, message: str, field: str, *, source: str):
        self.field = field
        self.source = source
        super().__init__(message)


def report_type_error(exc: Exception) -> None:
    print(f"Invalid configuration: {exc}")


def report_valid_value() -> None:
    print("Configuration value has the expected type")


def read_database_url(value: object) -> str:
    return ensure_type(
        value,
        str,
        "database_url must be a string",
        raise_exc_class=TypeValidationError,
        raise_args=["database_url"],
        raise_kwargs={"source": "environment"},
        do_except=report_type_error,
        do_else=report_valid_value,
    )


class TypeValidationBuzzError(Buzz):
    def __init__(self, message: str, field: str, *, source: str, base_message: str | None = None):
        self.field = field
        self.source = source
        super().__init__(message, base_message=base_message)


def read_database_url_with_buzz(value: object) -> str:
    return TypeValidationBuzzError.ensure_type(
        value,
        str,
        "database_url must be a string",
        raise_args=["database_url"],
        raise_kwargs={"source": "environment"},
        do_except=report_type_error,
        do_else=report_valid_value,
    )

On mismatch, each form constructs its configured exception with the field and source, passes that exception to report_type_error, then raises it. On a match, report_valid_value runs and the value is returned with its narrowed type. The standalone function also accepts exc_builder; the Buzz method binds the exception class and builder.
path: Ensure a value has the right type

items.title: Handle errors in a context manager
items.text: The handle_errors() context manager catches exceptions raised inside a block and re-raises them as another exception type. The new exception's message includes the original message.

items.title: Synchronous use
items.text:
from buzz import handle_errors

# Vanilla python
try:
    this_could_fail()
    this_could_also_fail()
    this_will_definitely_fail()
except Exception as err:
    raise RuntimeError(f"Something didn't work -- Error: {err}")

# With py-buzz
with handle_errors("Something didn't work", raise_exc_class=RuntimeError):
    this_could_fail()
    this_could_also_fail()
    this_will_definitely_fail()

This context manager trims some repeated exception-handling code. For more involved handling, a standard try/except block may be a better fit. A Buzz subclass method binds the exception type for you:

from buzz import Buzz, handle_errors

class ConfigError(Buzz):
    pass

with handle_errors("Could not load configuration", raise_exc_class=ConfigError):
    load_config()

with ConfigError.handle_errors("Could not load configuration"):
    load_config()

items.title: Advanced use
items.text:
Filters decide which failures are wrapped. In synchronous use, callbacks receive the original failure context, and constructor arguments are passed to the replacement exception:

from buzz import Buzz, DoExceptParams, handle_errors


class DataException(Exception):
    def __init__(self, message: str, dataset: str, *, source: str):
        self.dataset = dataset
        self.source = source
        super().__init__(message)


def report_error(params: DoExceptParams) -> None:
    print(f"{params.base_message}: {params.err}")
    print(params.final_message)


def report_success() -> None:
    print("Data loaded")


def close_data_source() -> None:
    print("Data source closed")


def load_data() -> None:
    with handle_errors(
        "Could not load customer data",
        raise_exc_class=DataException,
        raise_args=["customers"],
        raise_kwargs={"source": "warehouse"},
        handle_exc_class=Exception,
        ignore_exc_class=RuntimeError,
        do_except=report_error,
        do_else=report_success,
        do_finally=close_data_source,
    ):
        read_customer_rows()


class DataError(Buzz):
    def __init__(self, message: str, dataset: str, *, source: str, base_message: str | None = None):
        self.dataset = dataset
        self.source = source
        super().__init__(message, base_message=base_message)


def load_data_with_buzz() -> None:
    with DataError.handle_errors(
        "Could not load customer data",
        raise_args=["customers"],
        raise_kwargs={"source": "warehouse"},
        handle_exc_class=Exception,
        ignore_exc_class=RuntimeError,
        do_except=report_error,
        do_else=report_success,
        do_finally=close_data_source,
    ):
        read_customer_rows()

Both contexts wrap exceptions that are instances of Exception and not RuntimeError (or its subclasses) as their configured exception. report_error receives a DoExceptParams object containing err, base_message, final_message, and trace. do_else runs only when the block succeeds. Only the standalone function accepts raise_exc_class; the Buzz method binds the class and uses re_raise=False to absorb handled errors.

items.title: Async use
items.text:
The async form also accepts synchronous callbacks, and can await async callbacks. Here do_except is an actual async callback; it receives the same DoExceptParams object:

from buzz import Buzz, DoExceptParams, handle_errors_async


async def record_failure(params: DoExceptParams) -> None:
    await write_audit_event(params.final_message)


async def fetch_data() -> bytes:
    async with handle_errors_async(
        "Could not fetch report",
        raise_exc_class=RuntimeError,
        handle_exc_class=(ConnectionError, TimeoutError),
        do_except=record_failure,
    ):
        return await fetch_report()


class FetchError(Buzz):
    pass


async def fetch_data_with_buzz() -> bytes:
    async with FetchError.handle_errors_async(
        "Could not fetch report",
        handle_exc_class=(ConnectionError, TimeoutError),
        do_except=record_failure,
    ):
        return await fetch_report()

The standalone synchronous handle_errors() accepts raise_exc_class; setting it to None absorbs a caught exception after the callbacks run. The Buzz methods do not accept raise_exc_class; use re_raise=False to absorb handled exceptions. By default, the context handles Exception and its subclasses, not BaseException subclasses such as KeyboardInterrupt or SystemExit.

items.title: Other functions
items.text: This guide covers exception utilities and retry decorators, including their standalone and Buzz subclass forms.

items.title: Get a traceback
items.text: get_traceback() fetches the current traceback from sys.exc_info. Buzz uses it internally, but it can be useful in other contexts too.

items.title: Basic use
items.text:
The standalone function and a Buzz subclass method both return the active exception's traceback. Call either one inside an except block:

from buzz import Buzz, get_traceback

class ConfigError(Buzz):
    pass

try:
    load_config()
except OSError:
    trace = get_traceback()

try:
    load_config()
except OSError:
    trace = ConfigError.get_traceback()

items.title: Reformat an exception
items.text: The handle_errors() context manager uses reformat_exception() internally, though it can be handy elsewhere too. It wraps an exception message in a more informative block of text. This remains a standalone utility; it has no Buzz class method.

items.title: Basic use
items.text:
from buzz import Buzz, reformat_exception

class ConfigError(Buzz):
    pass

err = ConfigError("Configuration is invalid")
print(reformat_exception("Could not load configuration", err))

The output looks like this:

Could not load configuration -- ConfigError: Configuration is invalid

items.title: Retry decorators
items.text: ConfigError.retry() and ConfigError.retry_async() retry synchronous and asynchronous functions when they raise selected exceptions. Retries can smooth over transient failures in network calls, APIs, and other unreliable operations.

items.title: Standalone decorators
items.text:
A custom Buzz subclass isn't required. The standalone decorators live in buzz.tools and use Exception by default; raise_exc_class can point them at another exception type:

from buzz.tools import retry, retry_async


@retry("Request failed after {attempts} attempts", retry_on=TimeoutError, raise_exc_class=RuntimeError)
def fetch_data():
    return make_request()


@retry_async("Request failed after {attempts} attempts", retry_on=TimeoutError, raise_exc_class=RuntimeError)
async def fetch_data_async():
    return await make_request_async()

The remaining retry options work the same as they do with a subclass's .retry() and .retry_async() methods.

items.title: Basic use
items.text:
from buzz import Buzz

class ConfigError(Buzz):
    pass


# Vanilla Python
def fetch_data(url):
    max_attempts = 3
    for attempt in range(max_attempts):
        try:
            response = requests.get(url)
            response.raise_for_status()
            return response.json()
        except (ConnectionError, TimeoutError) as e:
            if attempt == max_attempts - 1:
                raise
            time.sleep(2 ** attempt)  # Exponential backoff

# With py-buzz
@ConfigError.retry("Failed to fetch data after {attempts} attempts", max_attempts=3, backoff=2.0, retry_on=(ConnectionError, TimeoutError))
def fetch_data(url):
    response = requests.get(url)
    response.raise_for_status()
    return response.json()

items.title: Advanced use
items.text:
The retry decorators control which failures trigger another attempt, how long to wait, and what to raise after the final failure. max_attempts includes the initial call; backoff grows the delay exponentially, max_delay caps it, and jitter randomizes each delay between zero and the calculated cap. Disable jitter here to make the timing predictable.

from buzz.tools import ExcBuilderParams, retry


def build_retry_error(params: ExcBuilderParams) -> RuntimeError:
    return params.raise_exc_class(f"Retry limit reached: {params.message}")


def log_retry(attempt: int, exc: BaseException) -> None:
    print(f"Retry {attempt} after {type(exc).__name__}: {exc}")


@retry(
    "Report request failed after {attempts} attempts",
    max_attempts=4,
    backoff=2.0,
    max_delay=3.0,
    jitter=False,
    retry_on=(ConnectionError, TimeoutError),
    raise_exc_class=RuntimeError,
    exc_builder=build_retry_error,
    on_retry=log_retry,
)
def fetch_report() -> bytes:
    return request_report()

This standalone buzz.tools.retry form waits 1, 2, then 3 seconds between failed attempts, retries only connection and timeout errors, and logs before each retry. After four failed attempts, it raises a RuntimeError; the final exception is chained from the last triggering exception, so its __cause__ retains the last failure.

A Buzz subclass method binds the final exception type and builder. It still accepts the retry controls, callback, and constructor arguments:

from buzz import Buzz


class ServiceError(Buzz):
    def __init__(self, message: str, service: str, *, request_id: str, base_message: str | None = None):
        self.service = service
        self.request_id = request_id
        super().__init__(message, base_message=base_message)


@ServiceError.retry(
    "Inventory lookup failed after {attempts} attempts",
    max_attempts=3,
    backoff=1.5,
    max_delay=2.0,
    jitter=True,
    retry_on=TimeoutError,
    raise_args=["inventory"],
    raise_kwargs={"request_id": "req-42"},
    on_retry=log_retry,
)
def lookup_inventory() -> dict[str, int]:
    return request_inventory()

The default retry_on=Exception catches Exception and its subclasses, not subclasses of BaseException such as KeyboardInterrupt or SystemExit. Exceptions outside the selected retry_on types pass through immediately.

items.title: Asynchronous retries
items.text:
retry_async and .retry_async() use asyncio.sleep() between attempts. Their on_retry callback remains synchronous, even when decorating an async function:

from buzz.tools import retry_async


@retry_async(
    "Async request failed after {attempts} attempts",
    max_attempts=3,
    backoff=2.0,
    max_delay=2.5,
    jitter=False,
    retry_on=(ConnectionError, TimeoutError),
    raise_exc_class=RuntimeError,
    exc_builder=build_retry_error,
    on_retry=log_retry,
)
async def fetch_report_async() -> bytes:
    return await request_report_async()


class AsyncServiceError(Buzz):
    def __init__(self, message: str, service: str, *, request_id: str, base_message: str | None = None):
        self.service = service
        self.request_id = request_id
        super().__init__(message, base_message=base_message)


@AsyncServiceError.retry_async(
    "Async inventory lookup failed after {attempts} attempts",
    max_attempts=3,
    backoff=2.0,
    max_delay=2.5,
    jitter=False,
    retry_on=TimeoutError,
    raise_args=["inventory"],
    raise_kwargs={"request_id": "req-43"},
    on_retry=log_retry,
)
async def lookup_inventory_async() -> dict[str, int]:
    return await request_inventory_async()

Both standalone decorators are imported from buzz.tools. They accept raise_exc_class and exc_builder; the Buzz methods bind those automatically. All forms accept raise_args, raise_kwargs, and a synchronous on_retry callback.

items.title: Raise an exception from another
items.text: When exception handling is already in your hands, raise_from() is an alternative to the handle_errors() context manager. The new exception keeps the original as its cause, so Python's traceback shows both errors.

items.title: Basic use
items.text:
from buzz import raise_from

try:
    load_profile()
except OSError as err:
    raise_from("Could not load profile", err, raise_exc_class=RuntimeError)

The default message includes the base message, the original exception type, and its message.

items.title: With a Buzz subclass
items.text:
For a Buzz subclass, its class method raises an instance of that exception type, without passing raise_exc_class:

from buzz import Buzz


class ProfileError(Buzz):
    pass


try:
    load_profile()
except OSError as err:
    ProfileError.raise_from("Could not load profile", err)

items.title: Advanced use
items.text:
Both forms accept a final message, an explicit traceback, and extra constructor arguments. The standalone function also accepts a custom exception builder. In either case, the original exception remains the new exception's __cause__:

from buzz import Buzz, raise_from
from buzz.tools import ExcBuilderParams


# Standalone custom builder
def build_profile_error(params: ExcBuilderParams) -> RuntimeError:
    return params.raise_exc_class(
        f"{params.message} (store={params.raise_args[0]}, region={params.raise_kwargs['region']})"
    )


def load_with_standalone() -> None:
    try:
        load_profile()
    except OSError as err:
        original = err
        try:
            raise_from(
                "Could not load profile",
                err,
                raise_exc_class=RuntimeError,
                raise_args=["profile-store"],
                raise_kwargs={"region": "west"},
                exc_builder=build_profile_error,
                final_message="Profile storage is unavailable",
                trace=err.__traceback__,
            )
        except RuntimeError as wrapped:
            assert wrapped.__cause__ is original
            raise


# Buzz subclass with its own constructor
class ProfileError(Buzz):
    def __init__(self, message: str, store: str, *, region: str, base_message: str | None = None):
        self.store = store
        self.region = region
        super().__init__(message, base_message=base_message)


def load_with_buzz_class() -> None:
    try:
        load_profile()
    except OSError as err:
        original = err
        try:
            ProfileError.raise_from(
                "Could not load profile",
                err,
                raise_args=["profile-store"],
                raise_kwargs={"region": "west"},
                final_message="Profile storage is unavailable",
                trace=err.__traceback__,
            )
        except ProfileError as wrapped:
            assert wrapped.__cause__ is original
            raise

trace=err.__traceback__ explicitly attaches the original traceback; when omitted, the helper uses the active exception's traceback. final_message replaces the formatted default when it is a non-empty string. raise_args and raise_kwargs are passed to the exception constructor after the message.

items.title: Require a condition
items.text: require_condition() checks a condition and raises an exception when it fails. It saves you from scattering the same if <whatever>: raise Exception(<message>) pattern throughout your code, with a little less repetition.

items.title: Basic use
items.text:
from buzz import require_condition

# Vanilla python
if not some_condition():
    raise Exception("some_condition failed")

# With py-buzz
require_condition(some_condition(), "some_condition failed")

It is a small bit of syntactic sugar, but it can make functions with lots of checks easier to read.

For a Buzz subclass, the class method binds the exception type:

from buzz import Buzz, require_condition

class ConfigError(Buzz):
    pass

require_condition(config_is_valid(), "Invalid configuration", raise_exc_class=ConfigError)
ConfigError.require_condition(config_is_valid(), "Invalid configuration")

items.title: Advanced use
items.text:
Use callbacks to observe both outcomes, and constructor arguments to attach structured context to the failure. The standalone function takes an explicit exception class; a Buzz subclass method binds its own type and builder:

from buzz import Buzz, require_condition


class ConfigException(Exception):
    def __init__(self, message: str, setting: str, *, source: str):
        self.setting = setting
        self.source = source
        super().__init__(message)


def report_failure(exc: Exception) -> None:
    print(f"Configuration check failed: {exc}")


def report_success() -> None:
    print("Configuration is valid")


def check_config(enabled: bool) -> None:
    require_condition(
        enabled,
        "Configuration is disabled",
        raise_exc_class=ConfigException,
        raise_args=["feature flag"],
        raise_kwargs={"source": "startup"},
        do_except=report_failure,
        do_else=report_success,
    )


class ConfigError(Buzz):
    def __init__(self, message: str, setting: str, *, source: str, base_message: str | None = None):
        self.setting = setting
        self.source = source
        super().__init__(message, base_message=base_message)


def check_config_with_buzz(enabled: bool) -> None:
    ConfigError.require_condition(
        enabled,
        "Configuration is disabled",
        raise_args=["feature flag"],
        raise_kwargs={"source": "startup"},
        do_except=report_failure,
        do_else=report_success,
    )

When enabled is false, each function constructs its configured exception with setting="feature flag" and source="startup", calls report_failure with that exception, and then raises it. When it is true, report_success runs and the check returns normally.

items.title: exc_builder
items.text:
A custom builder can adapt an exception whose constructor does not accept the message first. It receives ExcBuilderParams, including the selected exception class, message, positional arguments, and keyword arguments:

from buzz import require_condition
from buzz.tools import ExcBuilderParams


class StatusError(Exception):
    def __init__(self, status_code: int, *, detail: str, source: str):
        self.status_code = status_code
        self.detail = detail
        self.source = source
        super().__init__(detail)


def build_status_error(params: ExcBuilderParams) -> Exception:
    return params.raise_exc_class(
        *params.raise_args,
        detail=params.message,
        **params.raise_kwargs,
    )


require_condition(
    False,
    "The account is inactive",
    raise_exc_class=StatusError,
    raise_args=[403],
    raise_kwargs={"source": "account check"},
    exc_builder=build_status_error,
)

The builder maps the check's message to detail, while raise_args supplies status_code and raise_kwargs supplies source. This example uses a local non-Buzz exception rather than assuming a particular web framework's constructor.

A Buzz subclass binds its own builder for the equivalent class-method call. Override exc_builder on the class to adapt its nonstandard constructor:

from typing_extensions import Self

from buzz import Buzz, require_condition
from buzz.tools import ExcBuilderParams


class AccountError(Buzz):
    def __init__(self, status_code: int, *, detail: str, source: str, base_message: str | None = None):
        self.status_code = status_code
        self.detail = detail
        self.source = source
        super().__init__(detail, base_message=base_message)

    @classmethod
    def exc_builder(cls, params: ExcBuilderParams) -> Self:
        return cls(
            *params.raise_args,
            detail=params.message,
            base_message=params.base_message,
            **params.raise_kwargs,
        )


AccountError.require_condition(
    False,
    "The account is inactive",
    raise_args=[403],
    raise_kwargs={"source": "account check"},
)

items.title: Verify a literal value
items.text:
verify_literal() checks a value against a typing.Literal type and raises an exception if the value is not allowed. Like ensure_type(), it returns the value on success, so it fits naturally into an expression.

The verify_literal() function uses TypeForm to narrow the type of the return value, so type checkers will accept the verified string as an instance of the string literal.

items.title: Basic use
items.text:
from typing import Literal, cast

from buzz import verify_literal

Species = Literal["jawa", "ewok", "pyke"]

# Vanilla python
def vanilla(val: str) -> Species:
    if val not in ("jawa", "ewok", "pyke"):
        raise Exception("Received an unexpected value!")
    return cast(Species, val)

# With py-buzz
def buzzy(val: str) -> Species:
    return verify_literal(val, Literal["jawa", "ewok", "pyke"])

A Buzz subclass method also binds the exception type:

from typing import Literal

from buzz import Buzz, verify_literal

Species = Literal["jawa", "ewok", "pyke"]


class ConfigError(Buzz):
    pass


def buzzy(val: str) -> Species:
    return ConfigError.verify_literal(val, Species)

items.title: Advanced use
items.text:
Both forms return the accepted value, run do_else on success, and pass the exception being raised to do_except on an invalid value. Constructor arguments can attach context to the error:

from typing import Literal

from buzz import Buzz, verify_literal

Species = Literal["jawa", "ewok", "pyke"]


class SpeciesError(Exception):
    def __init__(self, message: str, species_code: int, *, field: str):
        self.species_code = species_code
        self.field = field
        super().__init__(message)


def record_rejection(exc: Exception) -> None:
    print(f"Rejected unknown species: {exc}")


def record_accepted() -> None:
    print("Well known species accepted")


def parse_species(species: str) -> Species:
    return verify_literal(
        species,
        Species,
        "Unknown species",
        raise_exc_class=SpeciesError,
        raise_args=[400],
        raise_kwargs={"field": "species"},
        do_except=record_rejection,
        do_else=record_accepted,
    )


class SpeciesBuzzError(Buzz):
    def __init__(
        self,
        message: str,
        species_code: int,
        *,
        field: str,
        base_message: str | None = None,
    ):
        self.species_code = species_code
        self.field = field
        super().__init__(message, base_message=base_message)


def parse_species_with_buzz(species: str) -> Species:
    return SpeciesBuzzError.verify_literal(
        species,
        Species,
        "Unknown species",
        raise_args=[400],
        raise_kwargs={"field": "species"},
        do_except=record_rejection,
        do_else=record_accepted,
    )

For an unknown value, each form constructs its configured exception with species_code=400 and field="species", calls the rejection callback, and raises. For an allowed value, they call record_accepted and return it. A non-Literal type raises TypeError immediately. Python permits enum members in runtime Literal values, but verify_literal()'s current LiteralElement annotation excludes enums, so static type checkers may reject those annotations.
